speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER AS TO THE GERMAN OFFENSIVE.
speechtext:
I mentioned on Friday that I had sent a telegram to Sir Edward Kemp asking that we might be advised of the conditions wihich have developed in the German offensive, and I have a telegram from him this morning saying that the Canadians are not yet involved, and that he will keep us informed. The Minister of Militia and Defence (Major General Mewburn) has placed in my hands the latest official report which has been received and which reads:
Monday Morning Service.
Bulletin:
London, Mar. 26.-Fresh attacks by the Germans have developed northward and southward of Bapaume, the War Office announces. The British repulsed powerful attacks yesterday afternoon northward of Bapaume.
Bulletin:
Paris, Mar. 25.-The French on Saturday went to the assistance of the British and took over a sector of the battlefront, the War Office announces.
In the region of Noyon on the right bank of the Oise heavy fighting with the Germans is in progress.
Bulletin :
Paris, Mar. 25.- (Official)-The statement follows:
"French troops began to intervene on March 23 in the battle now being fought on the British front. They relieved certain of the allied forces and took up fighting themselves on this sector of the front.
"At the present time they are engaged in heavy fighting in the region of Noyon and they are disputing the heights of the right banks of the Oise with important German forces. ,
"Northwest of Rheims there has been a violent artillery action in the region of Courcy and Loivre. In the Champagne two German surprise attacks east of Suippe resulted in failure. French patrols took some prisoners near Tahure.
"There was much artillery activity between Arracourt and the Vosges. At daybreak German forces attacked the French lines east of Bleneroy and east of BadOnvillers. The Germans were repulsed with heavy losses."

London', Mar. 25.- (Official)-The statement follows:
"The battle continues with great violence on the whole front. Powerful attacks delivered by the enemy yesterday afternoon and evening north of Bapaume were heavily repulsed. Only at one point did the German infantry reach our trenches, whence they were immediately thrown out. Elsewhere the enemy's attacks were stopped by rifle, machine gun and artillery fire in front of our positions, and his troops were driven back with great losses.
"During the night and' this morning fresh hostile attacks have again developed in this neighborhood and also to the south of Bapaume.
"South of PeTOnne, bodies of German troops who had crossed the river between Lioourt and Brie were driven back to the east bank by our counter-attacks."
So far as one can judge, the Germans are undoubtedly throwing absolutely their full force into this attack. It seems to have been met with as great success as was anticipated from the first. It is beyond question that very much depends upon tihe issue; and I know the hearts of the people of the whole country will he lifted up in intercession that the right may prevail.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER AS TO THE GERMAN OFFENSIVE.
speechtext:
Intercession is very proper, but with the view, in a slight degree possibly of helping on the oause, I desire to ask the Prime Minister the following questions. Possibly he might be in a position to answer them to-day, but it will do no harm to ask them in connection with this matter. My questions are:
1.	Inasmuch as Canadians are engaged in the titanic struggle now going on for the preservation' of human liberty, is the Government taking necessary steps to maintain to the highest degree the pride, the courage, the resolution, the 'steadfastness and the confidence of the splendid and gallant soldiers of Canada, as well as of the Empire at large, in this struggle?
2.	Have the Government taken precautions in the management of the forces, the appointment and, the promotion of officers therein and the granting of honours, awards and decorations thereto, that favour from female, society, creed or other undue .influences, shall not prevail; but that all shall be awarded on the one basis of merit and fitness alone?

Sir John Macdonald accepted in the last resort, the principle of federative union. But it is only too true that in the years following Confederation, when Sir John - Macdonald was in office, he on 'many an occasion challenged provincial autonomy. I need only refer to the classical cases, if I may so term them, which were the bones of contention between the Dominion and the various provinces', notably Ontario, Quebec, Manitoba and the Maritime Provinces. Let me mention only a few of those oases to refresh the memory of the Provincial Rightists whom I see before me. There were the Insurance case, the Escheats case, the Liquor Licensing case, the Rivers and 'Streams case; and last, but not least, the famous Ontario, boundary dispute. 'In all those cases the uncompromising champion of centralization was Sir John Macdonald, and the uncompromising champion of provincial autonomy was Sir Oliver Moiwat. The provinces, and indeed, the Dominion, owe that great statesman a debt of gratitude for his unfailing devotion to the cause of provincial rights. His policy may toe summed up in, the one sentence: the provinces were sovereign in their authority in order to make Canada united in its diversity. That policy, Sir, which had as its champion the late Sir Oliver Mowat, rallied around it the prime ministers of the then existing province^', and many of the giants who played so prominent a part in the affairs of this country in the Dominion Parliament, notably the late Edward Blake, and my right hon. friend the present leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier).
That policy, Mr. Speaker, has been sustained by many judgments of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. The battle for provincial rights has been won. At least that was my impression, and it was the impression of the public, until the month of December 'last when, after the election, an Order in Council was passed by the present Government, which I shall read in.

a few moments. I may be told that the fact of our being at war necessitated extraordinary and drastic measures. It is true that we are at war. It is also true that drastic measures are sometimes necessary, provided, however, they are in keeping with the -spirit and within the four corners of the British North America Act, which is the Constitution of Canada. But the substitution of Orders in Council for Acts of Parliament on important matters such as the one to which I shall refer, is a dangerous weapon in the hands of any Government. The more dangerous is that weapon when such Orders in Council override, yes, directly override, the constitution. I claim that this is precisely what happened when in December last the Government attempted by Order in Council to control the borrowing powers of the various provinces of this Dominion. In order to make this point clear I shall quote the ipsissima verba of the Order in Council passed on the 22nd of December, 1917. It reads:
Whereas it is advisable that the Canadian investment market should' be conserved to facilitate the borrowing of the large sums of money that will be required for the prosecution of the war and to enable His Excellency's Government, if need be, to fully avail itself of the loaning capacity of the country for the paramount purposes of national defence, and that the impairing of the market should be prevented: by forbidding the offering and sale thereon of securities for raising money for purposes the execution of which may in the public interest be postponed until peace has [DOT]been restored, provision toeing made for the issue by the Minister of Finance of a certificate permitting the offering and sale of such securities as the said Minister shall dieem proper to except from such prohibiten;
Therefore His Excellency the Governor General in Council on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance and under the provisions of The War Measures Act, 1914., is pleased to enact the following regulations and the same are hereby made and enacted accordingly :
1. It shall he unlawful within Canada, hy or on behalf of any provincial, colonial or foreign government, municipality, commission, local government, institution, corporation or incorporated company, to issue, sell, offer or advertise for sale, any bonds, debentures or other securities evidencing an obligation to repay money borrowed, which may hereafter be issued by or on behalf of any such colonial or foreign government, municipality, commission, local government, institution, 'corporation or incorporated company as aforesajd, or any shares which may hereafter be issued of the capital stock, whether preferred or common, of any such corporation or incorporated company, or to purchase or agree to purchase any of the bonds, debentures or other securities or shares of capital stock aforesaid, unless the offering and sale thereof within Canada shall have 'been first approved by the Minister of

Finance by his certificate of approval in writing:
Provided, that nothing herein shall affect the issue, offering, advertising, sale or purchase of any bonds, debentures or securities of the Government of Canada, or the trading in any bonds, debentures, securities or shares of capital stock, heretofore issued and placed upon .the, market, or which shall have been originally issued' and placed upon the market with the approval of the Minister of Finance evidenced by his certificate as aforesaid.
The Order proceeds to declare that it will be a criminal offence to ignore its provisions. Now, Mr. Speaker, I must express my surprise that this Order in Council was passed by a Union Government. I can well imagine old members of the Conservative party who form part of this Government, and who are disciples of the late Sir John Macdonald, appending their signatures to such an Order in Council; but I am surprised beyond expression to find that such staunch provincial rightists as some of the hon. gentlemen who compose the present Government should have given their assent to it. On the other hand, I am pleased to know, and I say it with pride, that the first voice raised against this encroachment on provincial rights, was the voice of the Prime Minister of Quebec. Immediately this Order in Council was passed, the Attorney-General of Quebec, Sir Lomer Gouin, speaking for his Government, used the following language:
That in the opinion of the undersigned, these regulations are beyond the powers of the Federal Parliament which could neither adopt them directly, nor delegate the powers to enact them to the Government of Canada;
That the effect of the said regulations is to restrict the rights, powers and prerogatives of provincial governments, and, in particular, of the government of this province, in so far as regards the matters which the constitution governing us confers exclusively upon them, and that nothing in the British North Amerioa Act, 1867, justifies such an encroachment;
That the Order in Council in question was passed without the government of this province having been informed thereof, and that the knowledge that it acquired of it was so acquired through the press.
That it is of importance to strongly protest against this manner of interpreting our constitution by the central government, and against this attempt to do away with a right exclusively belonging to the provinces.
For the above reasons, the hon, the Attorney General recommends:	1. That the
Government of Canada be informed that it is the intention of the government of this province to consider these regulations as illegal, unconstitutional, and in no wise binding on this province.
.2. That a notice be published in the Quebec Official Gazette informing the public that in the opinion of this government the said Order in Council, dated 22md December, 1917, concerning the issue of bonds and debentures in
Canada is illegal and unconstitutional as far as this province is concerned.
I do not know the nature of the other protests which came from the other provinces, but I am sure that the Government did receive protests from some of the western provinces. I know that there w.a,s one from Manitoba and one from Nova Scotia; probably there were others.
I agree with the opinion expressed by the Attorney General of the province of Quebec that this Order in Council of 22nd December encroaches upon the rights of provinces generally, and therefore is absolutely unconstitutional. I cannot for the life of me understand the reasons which impelled the Government to act in that drastic fashion towards the Provincial Governments. The Order in Council was passed, immediately after the Victory loan, was launched and after all provincial governments had in every particular co-operated with the Minister of Finance to make that loan a success. Speaking of my own native province, I may say that the Government ,of Quebec subscribed a very large amount to the Victory loan-in the neighbourhood of 11,000,000, I believe. I may ibe wrong as to the figure, but in any case it was a very large sum. I cannot too- strongly-how shall I say it-denounce the manner in which this Order was passed and made public. No notice was given,; no consultation with provincial executives was had. I honestly believe that in this very serious time of financial stress through which we are passing, no better means could have been devised to impair and to shatter the credit of the provinces on the foreign markets.
I submit, then,, that this Order in Council constitutes ,an encroachment on provincial rights1. Wihat .is the guiding principle in the matter of the borrowing powers of the Dominion Government and the provincial legislatures respectively? By section 91, subsection 4, of the British North Am&riea Act, the Dominion Government is given, it [DOT]is true, exclusive legislative authority with respect to the borrowing of money on the public credit. Though general in,terms, this expression, "the borrowing of money on the public credit," must manifestly be, and, I submit, is, restricted by the context. How is it so restricted? In the enumeration of the executive powers of the provincial legislatures-section 92, subsection 3 of the British North America Act-we read the following: "The borrowing of money on the sole credit of the province." Mr. Speaker, il w-ish to say a few words in support of the motion. I do not intend to deal with the constitutional question but there is another point of view to which I desire to draw the attention of the

members of this House. The preamble of this Order in Council says:
Whereas it is advisable that the Canadian investment market should he conserved to facilitate the borrowing- of -the large sums of money that will be required for the prosecution of the war, and to -enable His Excellency's Government, if need be, to fully avail itself of the loaning capacity of the country for the paramount purposes of national defence, and that the impairing of the market should be prevented -by forbidding the offering and sale thereon of securities for raising money for purposes the execution of -which may in the public interest be postponed until peace has been -restored, provision being made for the issue by the Minister of Finance of a certificate permitting the offering and sale of such securities as the said- Minister shall deem proper to except from such -prohibition-.
I quite agree, Sir, that -sacrifices of liberty, and -temporary suspension of laws can be justified when- they -are the result of imperious -and unavoidable necessities for nation-al defence. But, when they are not strictly based on -such considerations, and if they toe only the result of the natural tendency of all governments -to reach after additional power; if they he the immediate consequence of the executive's ecom -towards Parliament, provincial legislatures, municipal and similar institutions and the rights- of citizens, -then the -sacrifice of civic liberties and the suspension- of laws are without any possible excuse, and are illicit and worthy o-f blame. In European countries, where war exists, they have under similar circumstances for the salvation of the nation, suspended temporarily the application o-f certain laws, but they have never violated their constitutions. By this Order in Council our constitution is tom like a scrap of paper, as has been fully demonstrated toy my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux). Supposing for the sake of argument that this Order in Council is absolutely constitutional, was the Government confronted by perils and unavoidable exigencies- of national defence sufficient to justify it? To this question I believe we can answer in the negative. In support of this contention I will quote the opinion of a man whose judgment cannot be suspected of partisanship, and whose opinion is reported in The Montreal Gazette of March 21 as follows:
r
Toronto, March 20.-Judge Denton has decided in favour of the London Life Insurance Company in the action brought by Mrs. M. F. Skimin for $500, life insurance on her soldier son Private Garnet Redvers Skimin, killed in action July 25th, 1916. An appeal will be taken.
The question placed before Judge Denton was whether young Skimin was engaged in a military enterprise for the defence of Canada from invasion at the time of his death.

The Company claimed that within the terms of the policy Skimin was not so engaged, and therefore they were not bound to pay the amount of the policy.
Mr. Justice Denton, who rendered judgment in this case, is a member of the Supreme Court of Ontario. I concur in his [DOT]view when he holds that this war is not a military enterprise for the defence of Canada against the invasion of an enemy, and I believe that I am right in concluding that the motive of national defence invoked in the preamble of the Order in Council in question for the purpose of justification, is, unfortunately, not well taken.
Moreover, there are many other reasons which militate against this Order in Council. In the Order in Council provision is made for the issue by the Minister of Finance of a certificate permitting the offering and sale of such securities .as the minister may deem proper to except from such prohibition. How would that work, Sir? Either the sale of all such debentures will be authorized by the Minister of Finance, or authorization will be refused, or authority will be partly granted and partly refused, at the discretion of the minister. If the authorization for sale of all such securities is granted then this Order in Council is useless, and is only an encroachment upon the provincial autonomy, against which I strongly protest- If you interfere with provincial autonomy, Sir, you are going to break up Confederation, and that would be a national calamity.

speechtext: Before the election the Government promised the abolition of patronage. But now, by this Order in Council they have created a new source of patronage. Therefore, from whichever point one examines this question, one must conclude that the Order in Council which we are discussing is nefarious and contrary to the public interest and to sound principles of public policy. For the reasons I have' given, I, therefore, ask the Government to show that due respect for the law which is a guarantee of the peace, good order, liberty, prosperity and greatness of the nation. The Government must be the first to observe that respect, the first to present an example of proper regard for the Constitution. Otherwise the tampering, the manipulation, or, if you will permit me to use a French word the better to express my idea, the sabotage by the Government of the Constitution will tend, sooner or later, to bring about sabotage of the laws of the country by the people at large. I submit, Sir, that this Order in Council ought to be immediately repealed, because in my humble judgment it is an unqualified violation of the Constitution, an unjust encroachment upon provincial autonomy, harmful to Canadian credit and the development of our resources to their full extent, and because I am desirous of upholding Canadian interests above everything else and for all time.

maintopic: RESTRICTION ON SALE OF PROVINCIAL AND MUNICIPAL SECURITIES.

speechtext:
Mr. 'Speaker, the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Trahan) contends that this Order in Council was promulgated by the Government purely and solely for the purpose of invading the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures and of prohibiting school hoards, parishes and provinces from raising money by the sale of securities. The hon. gentleman left ime with the impression that it was his view that the Government had no other .purpose in the promulgation of this Order in Council than that .provincial and local interests should be harassed and their rights invaded. Of course, if my hon.

friend chooses to look at the matter in this, spirit he cannot possibly understand the reason or the purpose for which the ,Order in Council was passed. Personally, I cannot see why there should he any lengthy and serious argument upon the constitutionality of this Order in 'Council. I do not object to the provincial legislatures making their protests upon constitutional grounds; the matter may he debatable as a constitutional question. But I do say that in all the circumstances the provinces, having once stated their objection and expressed their opinion as to the constitutionality of the Order in Council, might well noiw let the matter there stand.
I do not agree with the hon. gentleman from Maisonneuve (Hon. Mr. Lemieux) when he says that the Order in Council was received with pain and surprise by the people of Canada. I deny that assertion. I have, during the past few weeks, come in contact with representatives of many of the provinces o,f Canada and have had expressed to me Iby members of provincial governments their approval of this Order in Council. In fact, I know of only one province in Canada which has gone to the trouble of expressing at length a formal protest against the OrdeT.
I refer to the province of Quebec-although the intention and purpose of tire Government in enacting this Order in Council having been explained, the Government of that province has, I think, also changed its view, if not from the constitutional viewpoint, at least 'from the practical standpoint.
Does the hon. member for Nicolet (Mr. Trahan) mean to tell me that the financial necessity of the country in these days should give way to small parochial and provincial interests? He states that the motive in passing this Order in Council was to attack the borrowing powers of school boards, parishes and provinces; that it is an attempt to break the constitution. Well, I do say this: in these days provincial and parochial rights must, if necessary, give may to national interests. It is more important to save this country than it is to save the borrowing powers of small borrowing bodies. This Parliament has no desire-neither has the Government-to invade the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures; but in these days the Government must, at many times, do things which in ordinary times it would not attempt.
Let me explain in a few words the reasons which impelled the Government to pass this Order in Council. In carrying on civil Government and paying for our participation in this war, we are necessarily

obliged to raise in one form or another a great deal of money. Hon. gentlemen know as well as I do that it is not possible tors-,ise the necessary large amount for these purposes by the ordinary forms of taxation. We must, in the first place, provide sufficient revenue to carry on civil Government, and, in the next place, raise sufficient revenue to pay for carrying on our part of the war. Not only that; we must provide from time to time credits for carrying on the trade and commerce-of the country. We could not export wheat; we could not export cheese; we could not export anything to-day unless the Government of Canada provided the financial resources or the credit in some form or other. In other words, the country must be self-contained financially; therefore, it is necessary that we be borrowers -within Canada and for large sums. With these huge commitments for the present and for the future, is it unreasonable to say by Order in Council-particularly when, we have the authority-that provinces, municipalities, companies and private individuals shall not issue and sell securities except by license of the Federal Government? It never was the intention of the Government that by this Order in Council provincial governments should be prohibited from borrowing upon the Canadian market. We realized that provincial governments could not go outside of Canada to borrow. None of the provinces can borrow to-day outside of Canada; neither can the Federal Government itself. When the Order was promulgated it became the policy of the Government to assist the provinces so far as they were unable to do so themselves by borrowing. Up to the present time one province has been loaned the sum of $2,500,000. The Dominion Government is also committed to make an advance of $3,000,000 to another province,, upon terms, of course. A province which could not borrow upon fair terms in this country to-day could not borrow outside.

We have made it known to all the provincial governments that in the event of their requiring to borrow any substantial sums of money and being unable to make favourable loans in Canada, we shall advance them the sums required for a period of five years at the rate [DOT]of six and one-half per cent interest, taking the obligation of the borrowing province therefor. Let me repeat that, so far as I know, no province in Canada, since being acquainted with the purposes for which the Government promulgated this Order in Council, has made any objection to it. It would be very undesirable and detrimental to the national interest to have municipalities or corporations selling on the Canadian money market large loans at low prices, which some would in many cases be obliged to do. This would affect adversely our market for Victory Bonds in the future. Last year over $400,000,000 was borrowed in this country by the Canadian Government, practically for carrying on our part of the war, by the sale of Victory Bonds. It will be necessary at the latter part of the present year again to appeal to the Canadian people for a similar loan, and by the same means. It is obvious, therefore, that if provinces and municipalities were allowed to go upon the market making loans at expensive rates, the market might be very seriously impaired for Federal purposes, when we again ask the Canadian public to subscribe to a further issue of Victoria Bonds for the purpose, really, of carrying on the trade and commerce of the country and for paying for our participation in the war. At least the Government is of the opinion it should have power to control the same if necessary.
Mr. Speaker, the argument made by the Minister of Justice convinces me that in the circumstances our jurisdiction is complete; that no constitutional argument can be urged against the validity of the Order in Council. As the Minister of Justice states that what we have done is to expropriate the money market of this country for Government purposes. We have not attempted to prevent provinces, or school boards, or parishes from issuing securities and selling them outside of Canada. We have not attempted to prevent provinces from imposing taxation for provincial purposes or anything of that character. All that we do say is that the Canadian money market may be necessary,
even for the preservation of our national life, and if that be so, the Government were and are now of the opinion that we should exercise the right, if we have the power, of controlling, until the termination of the war, the securities which will be placed upon the money market of this country, and I think hon. gentlemen, upon reflection, will be disposed to agree with that view.
In the exercise of the control of issues made by provinces or municipalities or corporations, great care should, of course, ibe exercised. So far, I do not think a license has been refused iby the Department of Finance. Our action, however, has had the effect that many issues would have been made were it not for the passage of this Order in Council; that is to say, that- many persons knowing that their proposed issues were of very questionable importance, and perhaps even detrimental, to the country at this time, have declined to proceed with their promotions of one kind or another, and consequently have refrained from appearing before the Finance Department to ask for a license to sell issues of securities or shares. I promise my hon. friend from Maison-neuve (Mr. Lemieux) that in exercising the discretion to refuse qr to grant a license to make issues of securities in this country the best judgment will Ibe used. I do not think that up to date any body, any person, or any province is in a position to complain of the exercise already made by the Government under the authority conferred upon it by the Order in .Council, and I do not think any opportunity will be given to make objection to the discretion which the Government may exercise in the future.

speechtext:
With the object which the Government may have had in passing this Order in Council, that is, to secure to themselves primarily and preferentially to anybody else the financial resources of the country, no one can find fault. I agree altogether with my hon. friend that it .is of the utmost advantage, and I would say more, even necessary, that the Government should endeavour to obtain for themselves, in preference to everybody else, what financial strength there is in this country. The only question is as to the method by which <the Government have attempted to carry out this purpose, which is laudable in itself.
5 p.m. They want to keep for themselves the available finances of *Canada. The question is whether or not they have, under our constitution, the power to deprive the provinces, and all the other bodies which derive their powers from

the provinces, of a similar advantage. My hon. friend has made a very complete and concrete case to the effect that the British North America Act specifically, in so many words, gives to the provinces the power to borrow. Section 92 of the British North America Act reads:
In each province the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated, that is to say,-
The borrowing of money on the sole credit of the province.
This is so clear that the Minister of Justice does not attempt to dispute it, but his answer to my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) in regard to this, was very technical and, might I say, sophistical. His whole argument was this, land nothing else: We do not propose and we did not intend to, and we did not, in fact, interfere with the powers of the legislatures to borrow; that is to say, notwithstanding the passing of this Order in Council, the legislatures have this power to borrow just the same as they had before. Of course, they have. But laws are passed to be executed; laws are passed to have their effect. The Legislature of Ontario or the Legislature of Quebec may pass a law to borrow money, but it cannot execute that law if this Order in Council places that power in the hands of the Dominion Government. Thus' the Minister of Justice leaves to the provinces a power which is barren and of absolutely no effect at all. Why was this power given to the provinces? Because it was well understood that the provinces in carrying out their undertakings might have to borrow, and if a province can pass laws, but cannot execute them, it is mere sophistry to say that the power of the province is not invaded. (If a province has the power to pass laws, but not the power to execute them, there is invasion of its power. The argument of my hon. friend iis simply sophistical, and it is mere playing with words to tell us that a legislature has power to pass laws which it cannot execute. speechtext:
It may he that under the constitution of the United States there is such a right, but any right hon. friend will not deny that up to the present the interpretation of the constitution of 'Canada has been that the legislative powers of the provinces were paramount within their .spheres' and that the legislative power iof the Dominion wias paramount in its isiphere. If that be the proper interpretation of the constitution, I claim that in this country we have no such power as any right hon. friend has just stated. My hon. friend isaid a moment ago that only the province of Quebec had protested. I think I am. right in saying that the provinces' of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Allberta have also protested in the same manner as the province of Quebec. But I shall be sorry to dispose of that question simply upon a technical matter of this kind. While I am altogether behind the Government in their endeavour to secure to themselves primarily and in preference to everybody else the financial 'resource's of the' country, the Government, In my estimation, acted very unwisely when they acted as they did.
If they had .consulted the provinces before, as they did afterwards, the question might have been settled otherwise and they would have obtained the unanimous consent of all the provinces. If they had said to the gov-

ernments of the different provinces, "We are to-day-in the midst of an immense danger, the cause for which -we are fighting is paramount, and everything must subside before it " the governments of the provinces would have been willing to stand behind them. If the Government had said to the provinces: " If you have to borrow money, we ask you not to borrow it .from outsiders but give ue the privilege of lending it to you,"' it would have been much better. They might have made the same suggestion to the municipalities. The Acting Minister of Finance said they would have lent the provinces the money themselves. If they had said to the provinces, "Do not got to market and try to borrow, but come to us and let ue assist you" that would have been the proper course, and I would highly commend the Government for taking it. My only regret is that they should have, in an unduly and in the most highhanded manner, attempted to override the power which the provinces acquired. We must avoid, as far as we can, all difficulties of this nature in normal times, and we must still more avoid them in wax times..

maintopic: RESTRICTION ON SALE OF PROVINCIAL AND MUNICIPAL SECURITIES.
subtopic: DISCUSSION ON ORDER IN COUNCIL PASSED BY GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to express my gratification that the leader of the Opposition thoroughly agrees with the policy which has been carried out, which was aimed at being carried out, under this Order in Council. The manner in which it has been done appears to be displeasing to some hon. gentlemen. The constitution would appear, in the words o.f the other speakers, to 'be in great danger, and, having been, for .many years, one of the men referred to by the hon. mover of this resolution, as strongly in favour of the maintenance of provincial rights and the careful guardian of constitutional privileges from the provincial standpoint, I feel that I should not neglect the opportunity, on hehal.f of the provinces of thanking the hon. , gentlemen- for the extreme interest which they now take in the rights of those provinces. There were times when we could not get quite such strong views from some of them, or even from- some of the members on this side of the House in regard to the rights of those provinces, and I am glad to say it is now generally conceded that the constitutional privileges of provinces should be recognized in all respects. In regard to this particular question the argument appears to be one that might more properly be addressed to the Privy Council when this question finally reaches there after the conclusion of the war. The brief that the hon. mover of the resolution had
prepared was an extremely good one. It was one that would be very useful in arguing legal questions, but as he himself recognized, it is possible to prepare a brief on both sides of nearly every constitutional question that has arisen since Confederation. There has never been any great difficulty in getting eminent legal gentlemen to prepare very excellent briefs on both sides of the many constitutional questions that he has brought to the attention of the House this afternoon, and there has been, on many of these occasions, a reference to the constitution of the United States. It is one of the favourite places to go for analogy. The constitution of the United States, of course, varies considerably from the constitution of Canada. Their constitutions are ever so much more exact in their wording, being all written, and not depending upon common law at all. It is very easy to argue in regard to what is done and what is not done in the United States. But even in the United States, when occasion arises, we find that the Federal Government assumes authority, as the Federal .Government does hereon occasion, and the framers of the constitution of the United States would probably have been much surprised if they foresaw that such powers would be assumed as have been assumed by the Federal Government, We find that when the United States declared war their President assumed the power, as a war measure, of confiscating hundreds of millions of dollars worth of property of individuals in the various states, and we find that only the other day the President of the United States assumed control of thousands of miles of railway that were chartered by the various states of the Union, and that were not under the Federal control. These, Mr. Speaker, are matters of the same nature as are provided for in the Order in Council that has been under discussion this afternoon, and while I am not going to discuss this matter from the legal .standpoint, as has been done so well by the Minister oif Justice and by the mover of the resolution, I say that in this- case, as in the oases I referred to, the Government of this country has only done what it was expected by every citizen of the Dominion it should do, to get the money that was actually necessary to conduct the war and to-carry on the affairs of this country. This course may properly be followed further, and it may have to be followed further, if this country is to do what is absolutely essential at the present time. The-question is vastly more important, even, for the provinces themselves and the various-

municipalities, than the purely technical question as to whether, for a short time, their powers have been infringed upon by this Order in Council. It is quite proper for those provinces to file a protest with the Minister of Finance in connection with this matter; quite proper for them from a purely provincial standpoint to see that their rights are not infringed upon in a permanent way without protest. I must differ from the right hon. leader of the Opposition in regard to what 'the proper course was, because not one of those provinces would haVe felt they were justified, if they had been asked previously, in giving up one jot or tittle of their provincial authority to the Federal Government. But, it being an accomplished fact, every one of those provinces, I believe, is prepared to join in heart and soul and assist the Minister of Finance in the getting of the money that is absolutely essential at this time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened very attentively to the remarks of the hon. Minister- of Customs (Mr. Sifton) and I must admit that his remarks somewhat surprised me, all the more so since he belongs to those western provinces for which the hon. leader of the Opposition did so much while he was at the head of the public affairs of this country.
The hon. minister felt called upon to reproach the hon. leader of the Opposition with having given expression, this afternoon to ,what is for him a new idea, the idea of protecting the autonomy of the Canadian provinces. I do not know if the hpn. minister has a short memory, or whether his knowledge of public affairs is not sufficiently wide, but despite my youth and my inexperience, and although I have seen less of public life than he, I remember, Mr. Shaker, the struggle carried on by the hon. leader of the Opposition for the autonomy of the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, at a time when his own province threatened to turn against him because of his principles. But the hon. leader of the Opposition on that occasion proved that he was not a politician who. varied his principles to suit the circumstances, but that, always, he guided himself and his party by the immutable principles of that Liberalism to which we belong this year, as we belonged last.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to answer the hon. minister in the English tongue, but I hope that he understands me when I say that we, the Liberals of the province of Quebec, were the first to fight for the liher-
	-
ties which his Government, a Government whose leader he remained until recently, have turned to their advantage.
NTr. .Speaker, I do not wish to retain the attention of this House very long. The main question brought up by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) was very ably discussed by the mover, as by the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty). But permit me, Mr. Speaker, as a Liberal, to say this; the question before the House today is not a new one. It is the great question which has been raised in all the centres of colonization where the English, after leaving the old land of liberty, came here, on Canadian soil, to open up to civilization a new domain.
When the American colonies struggled and fought against the central power, why did they do so? To try and prevent that central power from destroying the liberty of the individual states.
Here in Canada, there is not a man in this House who does not know of the struggles that were fought in the province of New Brunswick, in the province of Nova Scotia, before these provinces became a part of Confederation; neither is there here a man who does not know of the great 'Struggles that took place in this country before Confederation, and while Confederation was being formed, between the Liberals who wanted the provinces to safeguard their own liberty and the. Tories who wanted to centralize all authority in one government.
Mr. Speaker, Confederation was brought about. On what basis was it brought about? It was brought about on the following, basis, to wit: that we should have in this country two Governments; the Federal Government which was to concern itself with all questions of a general character and of a national character; and the provincial governments which were to look after matters of local interest, of a less general character. But, Mr. Speaker, we must not forget that the Act of Confederation is such that the provincial powers are as weighty within the provincial sphere as is the federal power within the federal sphere, and that the government of Quebec, the government of Saskatchewan, the government of Alberta are sovereign governments just as the Government at Ottawa may claim to be.
But, Mr. Speaker, allow me to say this in closing: The hon. minister appealed to the patriotism of those who listened to him. We, of the Opposition, just as much as our friends on the other side of this House, are in favour of the triumph of the sacred cause of the Allies. At this moment we are passing

through a solemn hour. We have as much unrest, as much anxiety in our souls and in our hearts as have our friends on the right. When millions upon millions of men are fighting on the soil of Europe to uphold what is most sacred and most cherished for us all, i.e.: the right to breathe in freedom; when in the old province of Quebec prayers ascend from every hearth for the triumph of the British flag which has given us the constitutional liberties which we enjoy; we must not, while we are laying down our lives, while our children are shedding their blood, we must not forget the fundamental principles which should always guide' the governments of this country; it must not be that while on the one hand we go to shed our blood for the cause of Liberty on the other, in our own country, the provinces lose their prerogatives.
Mr. Speaker, if the Government formed last year is always inspired by the lofty ideas and the great principles which presided at the birth of Confederation; if the Union Government lays aside a policy which sets the provinces against the federal authority and declares for a policy of veritable union, of true understanding, the nine provinces will stand behind it in the prosecution of this struggle which must lead to an ultimate victory, though it may be that just now we are experiencing a few hours of difficulty.
Mr. Speaker, the resolution of the hon. member for Maisonneuve shows that the Liberal party, in this matter, respects the high principles which presided at its birth, which have fortified it in it's struggles, and which allow us young members on this side of the House to hope that as long as these principles are not forgotten, we may perhaps suffer defeat, but the dawn of the morrow will always find us as strong, just as mighty, clothed in the principle which will have guided us thoughout the battle.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SUPERINTENDENT AND INSPECTORS.

speechtext:
On the motion of Hon. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice), the House went into
Committee on the following proposed resolution; Mr. Boivin in the Chair :
That it is expedient to amend the Penitentiary Act, Chapter 147, of the Revised Statutes, and to provide that the Governor in Council may appoint a Superintendent of Penitentiaries, who shall be an officer of the Department of Justice, and superintend the administration and business of the penitentiaries, and who shall be paid such salary as may be prescribed by the Governor in Council; land three Inspectors of Penitentiaries who shall be classified as officers of the Department of Justice, in sub-division B of the First Division of the Civil Service, and shall each receive a minimum salary of twenty-five hundred dollars per annum.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SUPERINTENDENT AND INSPECTORS.
speechtext: Will my hon. friend explain?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SUPERINTENDENT AND INSPECTORS.
speechtext:
The reason for introducing this resolution, upon which a Bill is to be founded, consists in the fact that it has been found necessary to provide salaries for the offices that it is proposed to create. The Bill, which will be founded upon this resolution, proposes to modify the present Penitentiary Act in this respect; Under the Act the chief officers in control and having direction of the penitentiaries are two inspectors holding equal rank and performing duties that would belong to an inspector proper, that is the inspection of penitentiaries, and the duty of directing and controlling, under the Minister of course, the administration of the penitentiaries. I have now been connected with the administration of penitentiaries for some few years, and I think I may safely say that in practical operation the system does not work out to the best advantage. It has appeared to me, and I hope when we come to deal with the measure I shall be able to carry conviction to the House, that we would get a more efficient administration of the penitentiaries if we separated the work of inspection from the work of management, control, and direction, taking the latter and putting it into the hands of one officer who, under the minister, would have the responsibility, and providing at the same time for an officer who would hold the title of inspector and who would in reality perform the duties corresponding to that title; that is to say who would inspect the penitentiaries, and report on their condition in order to keep the superintendent, and through him, the department and the minister in touch with what is going on within these institutions. The Bill itself contains provisions, following upon that change of system, with regard to the making of regulations and so forth, transferring in effect that portion of the duties of the present in-



specters which consists in the general direction of the penitentiaries over to the superintendent and making the modifications in the system which are necessitated by that transfer.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SUPERINTENDENT AND INSPECTORS.
speechtext: May I ask the minister in what respect he has found the present system deficient?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SUPERINTENDENT AND INSPECTORS.
speechtext:
It does not seem to me desirable that we should have two officers jointly, and upon a footing of perfect equality, acting in the direction of the penitentiaries. I think unity of control is highly important because it means unity of responsibility. There are great practical inconveniences from combining the duty of direction with that of inspection because the latter necessarily calls for absence from Ottawa. If you are going to have effective inspections of these seven institutions scattered over all the provinces you must necessarily have an officer in a position at any time it is thought desirable to proceed to these different penitentiaries and ascertain what is going on there.
There are advantages even in these visits, perhaps, being made not at stated periods when everybody expects the inspector, but in having all of the institutions in the position where the inspector may drop in at any moment. Now, it is, of course, impossible for the inspector to be in two places at once, "barring he was a bird," as one of my fellow-countrymen said, and we do find it necessary to have some one practically all the time in Ottawa to superintend, control and direct the management of these institutions. I venture to say that it is a more practical and businesslike method to have an officer to do the work of directing operations, and to have officers constantly available for the work of inspection proper. Inspectors, charged simply with the work of inspection, will, of course, not be held as of the same rank and importance as the superintendent or as the inspectors of the present day, and it will be noticed that we provide a smaller salary.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SUPERINTENDENT AND INSPECTORS.
speechtext: May I ask who the inspectors are at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SUPERINTENDENT AND INSPECTORS.
speechtext: The inspectors at the present time are Mr. Douglas Stewart and Brigadier-General Hughes. General Hughes is absent on leave, and has been absent since the outbreak of the war, serving his country in a military capacity. That fact, of course, has also hampered our operations-We have been trying to get on with one officer who has been carrying on the duties of superintendence as well as of inspection.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SUPERINTENDENT AND INSPECTORS.
speechtext: I have not the advantage of knowing Inspector Hughes, but I know Mr. Douglas Stewart very well, and he is a very competent officer, and if the hon..minister could show me and the House the importance of providing assistance to Mr. Stewart, I think it would go very far towards the very natural objection to increasing, at this time especially, the personnel of any department. Mr. Stewart has occupied his present position for more than twenty-five years, and he is one of those servants of the public who have given intelligence, zeal and honesty to the discharge of -all his duties, and if the hon. minister were to bring a report to the effect that Air. Stewart is suggesting this arrangement, for my part I should certainly be disposed to agree at once to the change.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SUPERINTENDENT AND INSPECTORS.
speechtext: I am not in a position to say that the change is the suggestion of Mr. Stewart. It is the result, as I said, of my own experience of the administration of these institutions since 1911, and when we come to deal with the measure itself-we are now dealing with the resolution principally with respect to the question of salaries-I hope to be able to satisfy [DOT] the House that the proposed system will prove a more effective one; and while it is true that it will operate to increase the number of officers dealing with this function, I may point out that it will not necessarily operate to increase in any material degree the expense of carrying on the work.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SUPERINTENDENT AND INSPECTORS.
speechtext:
I cannot see
that. At present, I understand, we have only two inspectors to do the work. Under this legislation you will have a superintendent of penitentiaries and three inspectors besides, making an increase of two in the staff.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SUPERINTENDENT AND INSPECTORS.
speechtext:
It is an increase of two in the staff, but the two present inspectors cost jointly $8,000. If we have but two inspectors-because we won't necessarily have three-at the salaries mentioned the cost would represent $5,000. If we pay the proposed superintendent the present salary of an inspector, the increase in expense would be only a thousand dollars. While there may be that extra expense, I do very confidently submit to the committee that there must necessarily be an increase of efficiency. It is not a matter of dealing with the personal qualifications of any one holding the office; I am speaking of the system. Where you have a system with one man charged with the direction and the responsibility, and where you have

people who may he thoroughly suitable people to do the inspection charged with the inspection, it does not necessarily follow that the qualities that make a good inspector make a good man to direct and control the administration of the penitentiaries. There is need, I may say, for an improvement in many respects in regard to the carrying on of the work of the penitentiaries, and probably of important changes with regard to the interior administration, more especially in connection with the work to be done by the superintendent. I arm satisfied, and I commend that view to the committee, that we will get a situation where it will be more easy to carry out a proper .system of efficient administration if we divide these two perfectly distinct classes of work, .and if we arrive at a situation where, fox the general direction and control, there is one responsible officer.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SUPERINTENDENT AND INSPECTORS.
speechtext: Did I understand the Minister of Justice to say that the two present inspectors are costing $8,000 and that the three inspectors will not cost any more, or did I misunderstand him?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SUPERINTENDENT AND INSPECTORS.
speechtext: I did not say they would not necessarily cost any more- I pointed out that the inspectors, if this Bill be passed, would be officers of a quite different class from the present inspectors, and that the salary, at all events the initial salary that is mentioned, would be such that two of these inspectors will cost but a thousand dollars more than one of the inspectors costs at the present time. That to get the better system it will probably cost something more I do not desire to dispute; but I feel very strongly that the better system, which I am .satisfied could be got by a reconstitution, is worth any increase that it may necessitate. I pointed out that, if we had but two inspectors under this new system, with a superintendent, and if the salary of the superintendent were fixed at the same amount as that of one of the present inspectors who exercise the superintending power, there would be an increase of a thousand dollars in cost.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SUPERINTENDENT AND INSPECTORS.
speechtext:
Whilst I agree with the leader of the Opposition that this is not the time for increased expenditure, I would forgive the hon. Minister of Justice if, in order to increase the efficiency of the administration of the penitentiaries, there would be, following the creation of these two new offices, some sort of prison reform in the Dominion. There is no doubt that *we have many more penitentiaries than we had at the time that Mr. Douglas Stewart
9i
was placed at the head of that service, and that the new provinces and the increased population have at least doubled the duties of that office. The point I wish to make is, that, if the creation of the new offices will give a better administration of the penitentiaries in the way of prison reform, I have no objection to the Bill. My hon. friend (Mr. Doherty) knows by past experience in this House that serious revelations have been made as regards the treatment of convicts in our penitentiaries which certainly drew from the Department of Justice very drastic- reports. I do not go as far as to say that the administration of our penitentiaries should be on a par with the new system at Sing Sing, where the Governor is the pal of all the convicts, although it has been found that that system has worked wonders in some cases.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SUPERINTENDENT AND INSPECTORS.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF SUPERINTENDENT AND INSPECTORS.
speechtext:
But certainly, and I am sincere in what I am now stating, there is need of more efficiency in the superintendence of the penitentiaries. Society is too apt to forget the convict once he has crossed the threshold of the penitentiary, whereas he should be followed into the institution and helped to become a man once more.
It was my good, or bad, fortune, some years ago, to visit the Kingston penitentiary, a splendid institution, but I was sorry on that occasion to notice a number of young convicts of about nineteen years of age associating with older convicts of the age of fifty, sixty, and seventy. I noticed, too, that these young men were breaking stones with the older convicts, and possibly learning by that association the tricks of much more serious crimes than had brought them within the penitentiary's gates. I would [DOT] point out, also, that there are methods of punishment inflicted on the convicts which are out of date, methods which, though quite proper in the middle ages, are in the present century antiquated and out of place. I repeat that if efficiency in the conduct of the penitentiaries will be increased by the appointment of the officers mentioned I raise no objection to the resolution. I sincerely hope that the Minister of Justice will respond to public sentiment on this matter, for that sentiment is not a fictitious one. I do not go the length of saying that you should allow associations of ladies to send flowers to men, condemned to death who are to be conducted to the gallows the next morning; but I say that there are certain means of improving the moral conditions of the convicts which ought to be appreciated by the superin-

tendient of these institutions. Undoubtedly iwe must change some of the methods now *in vogue for the sake of society and in the *best interests of those poor creatures who are unfortunate enough to be incarcerated within the walls of a penitentiary.
Resolution, read the first and second time, [DOT]and concurred in.

On motion of Hon. C. C. Ballantyne (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) Bill No. 15, to amend the Montreal Harbour Advances Act, 1914, was read the second time and the House went into Committee thereon, the Deputy Speaker in the Chair.
On section 1-C. 41 of 1914 amended so that advance of $9,000,000 may also be used to pay $300,000 of debentures maturing in 1918.

Will the minister
please explain?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
When this Bill was introduced, the member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) asked me to advise him what the programme of the harbour commissioners of Montreal would be for the season of 1918. Following the rigid policy ol economy that the Union Government is putting in force, I am holding down as well as I can the expenditure on the port of Montreal for the coming season. The harbour commissioners, subject to my approval, propose to spend during the coming season a total of only $220,000. Their intention is to continue the Montreal harbour system of railways further down the harbour in order to supply the various industries there and new ones which we hope will be located. That is estimated to cost $150,000. Then there is an amount of $15,000 for roadways and railway tracks on wharves. The dredging that will be required in connection with this extension of harbour railways is estimated to cost $50,000. Then there is $5,000 for electric system, power and lighting, making a total expenditure for the coming season of 
$220,000. In 1917 the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal spent a total of $705,000; in 1916, $1,237,918.31; in 1915, $1,922,581.69. The hon. gentleman will see, therefore, that the amount we propose to spend for the coming year is very small compared with the amounts spent in previous years. In addition to the $220,000 expenditure to which I have alluded, an amount of $300,000 will be available to retire the debentures that this Bill calls for.

The committee will be very much interested in the statement which has just been made by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. No work is more familiar to my hon. friend than the work of the Montreal Harbour Commission. Indeed, if I should express regret it is that my hon. friend is not still at the head of that commission rather than in the bad company in which he now finds himself. But, to be serious, while we are speaking of improvements at the harbour of Montreal, may I ask my hon. friend if precautions are being taken in all ports of Canada where munitions are stored to avoid any such disaster as that which occurred at Halifax last December? I am informed by an authority whom my hon. friend knows well- the harbour master of Montreal-that during several months of the year the city of Montreal is exposed to the same danger as that which brought about the disaster which took place at Halifax.
I myself have seen the shells and other munitions there. It seems to me that any such danger can be obviated if proper precautions are taken. The people of Montreal and of other ports through which shells are being shipped look upon the minister to prevent in the future the recurrence of what has happened in the past.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I deeply sympathize and so does the Government, with those who suffered by the terrible disaster which overtook the city of Halifax on December . 6th last. So far as the port of Montreal is concerned, one of my first acts when I became minister was to call the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal to Ottawa and to give them the most explicit and clear instruction that for the coming year no high explosive should he stored or loaded in the centre of the port of Montreal, or in what might be more properly termed the congested area. I have arranged that during the coming year all high explosives will be loaded many miles east of congested portion of the Harbour, in what is known as opposite Pointe aux Trembles. That is another reason why we are extending the

railway tracks down there. A special shed is being built for that purpose, and every precaution is being taken to avoid accident. I am also having expert navigators draw up very carefully prepared rules for the guidance of munition ships entering the port of Montrea/1 or any other of the seaports on the Pacific and Atlantic coasts. With the precautions that are being taken in the matter of loading high explosives and the providing of rigid rules for the guidance of munition vessels and all other ships entering seaports, we hope to avoid any such unfortunate disaster as that which took place at Halifax.
I observe that the first item of $150,000 covers the greater part of the proposed expenditure during next season. To what service will that item be specifically applied?

I am sure that though some people's memory may toe very short, he at least cannot forget that there was a time in his existence when he was a Reformer. One would almost thin'k that we were going through an absolutely normal period, one -would almost forget that we are passing through the most critical period, not only in. the history of Canada, hut of the Empire. We have been informed by the Finance Minister no later than to-day that we cannot borrow money in the United States or in England, and I know that we are not going to Japan, to the West Indies or to China to try and get it. We have got to raise whatever money we need in this country, and we will do so if the people are in a position to lend whatever money is needed. In view of the prevailing situation it becomes imperative for the new blood in the Cabinet-and there are good and earnest men there-to introduce reforms. Some of the old timber has disappeared, and although some of it is still left, it will disappear.

In connection with the engineers, I would like to bring a matter to the notice of the minister. We have in the Maritime Provinces a great many public wharves, breakwaters and structures of that kind, on which a great deal of money has been, expended, and these structures are very useful to the public. Repairs to those structures and wharves generally-almost always-awaited a report from the member. The member for the county would report to the engineer, or to the minister, that such and such a place required some expenditure. Very often that is neglected, and very often no attention is paid to the recommendation the member might make. It might he thought he was looking for patronage or the expenditure of money in his county. I would like the minister to make his engineers responsible for the upkeep of those structures. There are hundreds of thousands of dollars lost by reason of the fact that those structures are allowed to fall into decay and not properly looked after, and if the engineer is made responsible for the condition of those

works lie will be called upon to say what repairs are required, look after them, report them and have the work done, and prevent such waste as< I have mentioned, and the responsibility of reporting as to what may be required for improvements of that kind would not 'be thrown upon the member.

This is the first time 1 have ever heard the engineers criticised for not submitting reports to the department. I have not had time to read them all, I have tried to study up the items to some extent in preparing the estimates as printed. I have tried to listen to every hon. gentleman who has had a suggestion to make, although, I am sorry to say, during the last week I have not been able to find time -for all who wished to see me, but in the future I wili be only too happy to listen to the recommendations of any member of the House. I want to assure members, however, that after I receive their recommendations I shall invariably ask the engineer for a report. I have sent out to all engineers in Canada a circular letter informing them that when I ask for information I want facts, and we will draw the conclusions in the office, and I intend to act upon those recommendations just as far as it is possible to do so.
This raises the question which I might as well discuss" for a moment. Under the present financial conditions, as I view them, it is simply impossible to obtain money to be expended on public works that can be allowed to stand for. two or three years. I dislike turning down a request for a public work in any portion of Canada, as much as any naan who ever occupied this position. I would like to be able to go on and build. I think I could build in a fairly economical manner, but until such time as the financial condition of the country is different from to-day I do not feel justified in spending money on any public work that is not actually necessary. And, unless I change my mind very much, I do not think I will spend very much money during this year or next, except on the class of work I refer to. ,1 realize that very nice questions arise as to what is necessarily a public work, and possibly there might be a very

sharp distinction between my definition of the term and the definition suggested by other people in Canada. When that occasion arises we will have to apply to the engineers and exercise the very best business principles which we are able to command, and I want to assure the House that any decisions at which we arrive will certainly be along business principles, and also in accordance with the policy of not spending one dollar which the public service of this country can get along fairly efficiently without spending.
